title: String Quartet No. 16 in F major
hook: Beethoven’s last complete work, short and witty, ending with the question “Must it be?”

painting.title: Stein an der Donau
painting.pairingNote: The little town on the Danube below Gneixendorf, where Beethoven finished this quartet in October 1826 at his brother’s estate.

facts: Beethoven finished it in October 1826 at Gneixendorf, his brother Johann’s country estate on the Danube, where he had gone with his nephew Karl. It was the last major work he completed. Only a new finale for an earlier quartet, Op. 130, came after it. He died in March 1827.
After the long, unusual quartets that came before it, this one goes back to four movements and modest length, closer to Haydn and Mozart. It is the shortest of Beethoven’s late quartets.

Above the slow opening of the finale Beethoven wrote “Muss es sein?” (“Must it be?”), and above the quick answer “Es muss sein!” (“It must be!”). The phrase began as a joke: a music lover who wanted the quartet Op. 130 played in his home was told he must pay for it, and Beethoven wrote a comic canon on the words “It must be! Out with the purse!”. A later story about Beethoven’s housekeeper asking for her wages was invented by his biographer Anton Schindler.
He dedicated it to Johann Nepomuk Wolfmayer, a Viennese cloth merchant and a long-standing admirer. It was first played in public on 23 March 1828, at a concert in Beethoven’s memory.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a light, witty opening (I), a rough, wild scherzo (II), a slow song of peace (III), a question and its answer (IV).

movements.heading: Allegretto
movements.summary: A light, conversational movement in [[sonata-form|sonata form]]. Short scraps of tune are tossed from one instrument to another, more like a conversation than a melody with accompaniment.

mainIdeas.name: The opening figure
mainIdeas.description: a short, questioning phrase in the viola, answered by a little flourish in the first violin.

mainIdeas.name: The unison
mainIdeas.description: all four together in octaves, a few firm steps.

stops.hear: The viola alone plays a short, questioning phrase; the first violin answers with a tiny flourish
stops.happening: The opening figure, in F major

stops.hear: All four play firm steps together, in octaves
Lighter: quick rippling runs in threes, passed around
The scraps of tune go into other keys and are combined in new ways
The viola’s questioning phrase again, in the home key
The figures are packed more closely together

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The opening figure once more; a simple, quiet close

notice: Follow the opening figure. It rarely stays with one instrument for more than a few seconds.

movements.heading: Vivace
movements.summary: A short, fast [[scherzo|scherzo]] with a stubborn, off-beat rhythm. In the middle section the music climbs up through three keys, and then the three lower instruments repeat the same small figure, very loudly, for about fifty bars, while the first violin leaps wildly above them.

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo
mainIdeas.description: a simple tune that keeps tripping over the beat, the instruments seemingly out of step with each other.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: fast running notes in the first violin, climbing from key to key.

mainIdeas.name: The stuck figure
mainIdeas.description: one short, loud figure hammered again and again by the lower three.

stops.hear: A quick, simple tune with stubborn accents in the wrong places
Fast running notes in the first violin; the music lifts into a new key, then another
stops.happening: The [[trio|trio]], climbing from F to G to A

stops.hear: Very loud: the three lower instruments repeat one small figure over and over, the first violin leaps up and down
The quick, tripping tune again

stops.label: Last seconds
stops.hear: A quiet passage, then one sudden loud chord

notice: In the trio, count how long the lower instruments stay on their figure. Beethoven keeps it going much longer than you expect.

movements.heading: Lento assai, cantante e tranquillo
movements.summary: A slow, hushed song in D-flat major. In his sketches Beethoven called it a “sweet song of rest, or song of peace”. It is a theme with four [[variation|variation]]s, but the tune hardly changes; what changes is what surrounds it.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a slow, quiet hymn played low by all four instruments.

mainIdeas.name: The dark variation
mainIdeas.description: slower, in the minor, with broken, halting phrases.

mainIdeas.name: The cello’s turn
mainIdeas.description: the theme in the cello, almost unchanged, with the first violin imitating it a step behind.

stops.hear: A soft chord, then a slow, low, hymn-like tune
The first violin rises an octave, and the others follow
Darker, slower, in the minor: the phrases break off, almost into silence
Back in the major; the cello sings the tune while the first violin echoes it
The tune with gentle, broken figures around it; the cello moves in octaves

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The first violin climbs very high; a quiet chord like the opening one

notice: Listen to how little the tune itself changes. The variations are in the colour and the movement around it.
Compare the quiet chord at the very end with the one that opened the movement.

movements.heading: Grave, ma non troppo tratto – Allegro
movements.tempo: Grave, ma non troppo tratto – Allegro
movements.summary: Beethoven headed the finale *Der schwer gefasste Entschluss*, “The difficult decision”. A slow, heavy question in F minor (“Must it be?”) is answered by a quick, cheerful tune in F major (“It must be!”). The question returns once, louder, but the answer wins, and the quartet ends in good humour.

mainIdeas.name: The question
mainIdeas.description: three slow notes in the low instruments, in the minor, “Muss es sein?”.

mainIdeas.name: The answer
mainIdeas.description: the same three notes turned upside down and made quick and bright, “Es muss sein!”.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a light, tiptoeing tune, almost a march for fairies.

stops.hear: Slow and heavy: three notes in the low instruments, asked again and again
stops.happening: The question, “Muss es sein?”, in F minor

stops.hear: Quick and cheerful: the same three notes turned upside down
stops.happening: The answer, “Es muss sein!”, in F major

stops.hear: A light, tiptoeing tune
The quick answer again, from the beginning of the fast music
The figures are tossed between instruments and pushed into new keys
The slow question returns, now loud and more agitated
stops.happening: The Grave, more anxious than before

stops.hear: The cheerful answer, softly at first
The tiptoeing tune plucked, very quietly, like a music box

stops.label: Last seconds
stops.hear: “Es muss sein!” one last time, loud

notice: Sing the three slow notes of the question, then listen for how the answer flips them over.
The plucked passage near ≈ 6:45 is one of the most playful moments in all of Beethoven’s quartets.

threads.title: Back to the beginning
threads.body: After the vast late quartets, Beethoven returns to four short movements and the conversational style of Haydn and Mozart.

threads.title: Four voices
threads.body: The viola opens the first movement, the lower three drive the scherzo, the cello sings in the slow movement, and in the finale everyone takes part in the question and answer.

threads.title: A last word
threads.body: The question and answer were Beethoven’s joke, but his final completed work ends with “It must be!”. In Milan Kundera’s novel *The Unbearable Lightness of Being* the hero borrows the phrase.
